patient.name: Hannah Kowalski
patient.setting: GP surgery, then thyroid clinic and surgical ward
patient.complaint: A painless lump in the right side of her neck, growing for 3 months
background: Hodgkin lymphoma at 14, treated with neck radiotherapy

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with a neck lump: decide thyroid vs other (swallowing vs tongue protrusion), benign vs malignant (red flags), then the cancer type from age, spread and calcitonin.

points: Hannah, 34, noticed a **lump in her neck** while putting on a necklace.
Painless; it seems to have grown over 3 months.
Had **neck radiotherapy at 14** for Hodgkin lymphoma.
No weight change, palpitations or heat intolerance.

steps.lead: Hannah has a **discrete lump within the thyroid**. Most are benign, but her history means it must be assessed properly.
Hannah's **childhood neck radiotherapy** is the single most important risk factor for thyroid cancer.

points: A firm 2 cm nodule in the right lobe.
It **rises on swallowing** but **not on tongue protrusion**.
A hard 1.5 cm node in the right side of the neck.

steps.q: Which sign confirms the lump is in the thyroid, not a thyroglossal cyst?
o: Moves on swallowing but not on tongue protrusion
steps.r: The thyroid is attached to the larynx (moves on swallowing). A **thyroglossal cyst** also rises when the tongue sticks out.

steps.lead: Hannah's lump is lateral and does not move with the tongue, so it is not a **thyroglossal cyst**.
Like many nodules, Hannah's is **painless**. Hoarseness or dysphagia would suggest local invasion.
Hannah has two **red flags**: a growing nodule and a hard **lymph node**. Others: fixed irregular mass, hoarseness, weight loss.
A young woman with a solitary nodule and an **early nodal metastasis**: the pattern of **papillary carcinoma**.
Untreated, Hannah's papillary cancer would spread to **nodes and lungs**; follicular cancer goes through the blood to **bone**.

steps.text: Most thyroid nodules are **benign**. The exam tests whether you spot the red flags that change that.

investigation.exam: Expect 'next investigation': TSH first, ultrasound if TSH is normal, radionuclide scan if TSH is low, and FNA for a suspicious nodule.

steps.lead: Hannah's first tests are **TSH** and a **neck ultrasound** to grade the nodule's malignancy risk.

visual.label: Hannah 1.8

steps.title: Ultrasound report
steps.text: Every feature is suspicious: graded U5 (malignant appearance).

visual.label: Hannah U5

steps.lead: Hannah's suspicious nodule needs **FNA**: cytology comes back **malignant**, consistent with papillary carcinoma.

steps.q: A different patient's nodule comes with a **low TSH**. What next?
steps.r: Low TSH suggests an autonomous nodule: a scan shows whether it is **hot** (benign, functioning) or **cold**.

steps.lead: Hannah's TSH is normal so she needs no scan. A **hot** nodule is reassuring; a **cold** one carries more cancer risk.
Hannah's tumour is papillary, so she will be followed with **thyroglobulin**. **Calcitonin** is the marker for medullary carcinoma.

steps.text: FNA cannot tell **follicular adenoma** from carcinoma: invasion of the capsule or vessels is only seen on **histology** after removal.

management.exam: Expect reassurance for benign nodules, thyroidectomy then radioiodine for cancer, and the post-thyroidectomy complications (hypocalcaemia, hoarseness, haematoma).

steps.lead: Hannah's FNA is malignant, so she needs **thyroidectomy**, followed by **radioactive iodine**.

steps.q: What is the definitive treatment for Hannah's papillary carcinoma?
steps.r: Malignant nodules need **surgery**; radioactive iodine follows to ablate remnant tissue.

steps.lead: If Hannah's nodule had been benign, she would simply be **reassured and monitored**. A thyrotoxic nodule is treated with radioiodine or surgery.

steps.title: Management by result
nodes: Benign-looking in pregnancy → monitor until postpartum
Hot toxic nodule → radioiodine or surgery

points: Day 1 after total thyroidectomy and neck dissection.
Hannah reports **tingling around her lips** and fingers.

visual.title: Hannah's adjusted calcium after surgery
visual.caption: Parathyroid stunning drops her calcium; IV calcium gluconate then oral calcium bring it back.

steps.lead: Hannah's perioral tingling is **iatrogenic hypocalcaemia**. Her voice is checked for nerve damage and her neck for a **haematoma**.

steps.text: A tense, swelling neck with stridor hours after thyroidectomy is a **haematoma**: open the wound and **remove the sutures at the bedside**, before going to theatre.

steps.lead: Hannah's care follows the **British Thyroid Association** thyroid cancer guideline: ultrasound grading, FNA, surgery, then radioiodine.

steps.text: Post-thyroidectomy hoarseness = **recurrent laryngeal nerve**; perioral tingling = **parathyroids** (low calcium).

science.exam: Expect histology (Orphan Annie nuclei, capsular invasion), why calcitonin marks medullary cancer, and the anatomy behind surgical complications.

steps.lead: Hannah's case is the minority: most nodules are **colloid change, hyperplasia or adenomas**.
Hannah's histology shows **Orphan Annie eye** nuclei and psammoma bodies, typical of papillary carcinoma, which spreads via lymphatics.

head: Feature
Papillary

steps.lead: If Hannah's tumour had been medullary, it would come from **C cells**, so **calcitonin** would track it.
Hannah's tingling came from bruised **parathyroid glands**; the **recurrent laryngeal nerve** runs by the inferior thyroid artery.

visual.label: Hannah 1.92
visual.caption: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia: perioral paraesthesia and a positive Chvostek's sign.

steps.text: Medullary thyroid cancer is the one linked to **MEN 2** and **calcitonin**; it does not take up iodine, so radioiodine does not help.

prompts.q: What is a thyroid nodule and what are its risk factors?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: most are benign; know the risk factor.

points.p: Discrete lesion within the thyroid, benign or malignant
Most important risk factor: prior radiation exposure

prompts.q: What are the red flags for malignancy in a thyroid nodule?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem lists two or three.

points.why: Benign nodules are smooth and mobile.

prompts.q: How do you tell a thyroid nodule from a thyroglossal cyst?

points.p: Thyroglossal cyst is midline and rises on tongue protrusion

prompts.q: What are the four types of thyroid cancer and their key features?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: age and spread pick the type.

points.p: Papillary: commonest (~60%), women 30–40, early nodal spread
Follicular: older women, haematogenous to bone and lung

prompts.q: What is the investigation pathway for a thyroid nodule?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: TSH decides the next step.

points.p: FNA for large or suspicious nodules
Low TSH: radionuclide scan (hot = benign, cold = higher risk)

prompts.q: Which ultrasound features are suspicious, and how is medullary cancer followed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: three features and a marker.

points.p: Calcitonin: every 3 months for 2 years, then 6-monthly, then annually

prompts.q: How are benign, toxic and malignant nodules managed?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: match the plan to the result.

points.p: Malignant: total or partial thyroidectomy, then radioactive iodine

points.p: Wound haematoma: neck swelling 4–6 hours post-op; remove sutures immediately

points.p: Papillary: Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies
Follicular carcinoma vs adenoma: capsular and vascular invasion, on histology not FNA

glossary.thyroid nodule: A discrete lump within the thyroid gland; most are benign.
glossary.thyroglossal cyst: Midline neck cyst from the embryonic thyroid tract; rises on tongue protrusion.
glossary.papillary carcinoma: Commonest thyroid cancer; young women, spreads to lymph nodes.
glossary.follicular carcinoma: Second commonest thyroid cancer; spreads through blood to bone and lung.
glossary.medullary carcinoma: Thyroid cancer from C cells that secretes calcitonin; linked to MEN 2.
glossary.anaplastic carcinoma: Rare, very aggressive thyroid cancer in the elderly.
glossary.follicular adenoma: Benign tumour of thyroid follicular cells; looks like carcinoma on FNA.
glossary.colloid nodule: Benign nodule made of colloid-filled follicles.
glossary.FNA: Fine-needle aspiration: a thin needle samples cells for cytology.
glossary.cytology: Examination of individual cells under a microscope.
glossary.histology: Examination of tissue architecture, needed to see capsular or vascular invasion.
glossary.TSH: Thyroid-stimulating hormone; low in an overactive autonomous nodule.
glossary.radionuclide scan: Scan of isotope uptake showing whether a nodule is hot or cold.
glossary.hot nodule: Nodule taking up more isotope than the rest of the gland; usually benign and overactive.
glossary.cold nodule: Nodule taking up little isotope; higher malignancy risk.
glossary.hypoechoic: Darker than surrounding tissue on ultrasound; a suspicious feature.
glossary.microcalcifications: Tiny bright calcium spots on ultrasound; suggest papillary carcinoma.
glossary.spongiform: Sponge-like ultrasound appearance with many small cysts; a benign feature.
glossary.U score: British Thyroid Association ultrasound grade from U1 (benign) to U5 (malignant).
glossary.calcitonin: Hormone from C cells; tumour marker for medullary carcinoma.
glossary.thyroglobulin: Protein made by thyroid cells; used to monitor differentiated thyroid cancer after surgery.
glossary.parafollicular C cells: Neural crest-derived thyroid cells that make calcitonin.
glossary.MEN 2: Inherited syndrome of medullary thyroid cancer, phaeochromocytoma and (2A) hyperparathyroidism.
glossary.phaeochromocytoma: Adrenal tumour making adrenaline, causing episodes of palpitations, sweating and hypertension.
glossary.Orphan Annie eye: Clear, empty-looking nuclei typical of papillary carcinoma.
glossary.psammoma bodies: Round calcified bodies seen in papillary carcinoma.
glossary.capsular invasion: Tumour breaking through its capsule; defines follicular carcinoma.
glossary.thyroidectomy: Surgical removal of all (total) or part (hemi) of the thyroid.
glossary.radioactive iodine: Iodine-131 taken up by thyroid tissue; ablates remnants or treats hyperthyroidism.
glossary.recurrent laryngeal nerve: Nerve to the vocal cord muscles; damage causes hoarseness.
glossary.parathyroid glands: Four small glands behind the thyroid that control calcium via PTH.
glossary.hypocalcaemia: Low blood calcium, causing tingling, cramps and tetany.
glossary.perioral paraesthesia: Tingling around the mouth; classic sign of low calcium.
glossary.Chvostek's sign: Tapping the facial nerve makes facial muscles twitch; sign of hypocalcaemia.
glossary.haematoma: Collection of blood; in the neck after surgery it can compress the airway.
glossary.stridor: High-pitched noisy breathing from upper airway narrowing.
glossary.Hodgkin lymphoma: Lymph node cancer often treated with radiotherapy, raising later thyroid cancer risk.

technique.stem: A 32 year old woman has a 2 month history of a painless lump on the right side of her neck. She had radiotherapy to her neck as a teenager. There is a firm 2 cm nodule in the right thyroid lobe that moves on swallowing, and a hard right cervical lymph node. Her TSH is normal.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: A diagnosis question about a thyroid lump: decide if it is malignant, then which type.
Young woman, neck irradiation, solitary nodule with an **early nodal metastasis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Papillary carcinoma**: commonest, young women, lymphatic spread.

elim: Elderly patients with a rapidly growing, compressive mass.
Older women; spreads through blood, not early to nodes.
Needs calcitonin, MEN 2 or a family history.
Older women with Hashimoto's and rapid diffuse growth.

steps.x: **D. Papillary thyroid carcinoma.** Young woman + solitary nodule + cervical node = papillary.

technique.stem: A 45 year old woman has a 3 cm thyroid nodule. Her TSH is normal. Ultrasound shows a hypoechoic nodule with microcalcifications and irregular margins. She has no lymphadenopathy.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?

steps.x: 'Next' investigation after a suspicious ultrasound.
Normal TSH and three **suspicious ultrasound features**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Get cytology: **FNA**.

elim: Does not give a tissue diagnosis.
Only when TSH is low.
Delays diagnosis of a suspicious nodule.
Used for medullary cancer surveillance, not as the first diagnostic test.

steps.x: **B. Fine-needle aspiration.** TSH → ultrasound → FNA if suspicious.

technique.stem: A 51 year old woman had a total thyroidectomy 5 hours ago. She now has a rapidly enlarging, tense swelling in her neck and noisy breathing. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm, BP 142/88 mmHg and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Open the wound and remove the sutures at the bedside
Return to theatre at the end of the list

steps.x: Initial management of a post-operative emergency.
Neck swelling and stridor hours after thyroidectomy: **wound haematoma** compressing the airway.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Remove the sutures immediately** to release the clot.

elim: Wastes time while the airway closes.
Treats hypocalcaemia, which causes tingling, not neck swelling.
This is not bronchospasm.
Too slow; decompress now, then theatre.

steps.x: **D. Open the wound and remove the sutures at the bedside.** Post-thyroidectomy swelling + stridor = haematoma → open the wound now.

technique.stem: A 49 year old woman has a thyroid nodule. FNA shows a follicular neoplasm. She is told that the cytology cannot say whether it is benign or malignant and that the nodule must be removed.
technique.q: Which is the most likely reason FNA cannot make the diagnosis?
o: Malignancy depends on capsular and vascular invasion
Orphan Annie eye nuclei are absent in all samples
Psammoma bodies are destroyed by aspiration

steps.x: A mechanism question: why the test fails.

clues: cannot say whether it is benign or malignant
steps.x: Follicular adenoma and carcinoma look the same cell by cell.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Carcinoma is defined by **capsular and vascular invasion**, seen only on **histology**.

elim: That identifies medullary carcinoma, not follicular.
They are aspirated; that is how the neoplasm was seen.
That is papillary; irrelevant to follicular malignancy.
Papillary feature, not related.

steps.x: **C. Malignancy depends on capsular and vascular invasion.** Follicular: FNA can't distinguish; histology after lobectomy decides.

practice.stem: A 46 year old woman has had a small, soft lump in the front of her neck for 4 years that has not changed in size. She has no weight loss or voice change. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm and BP 120/76 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a 12 mm smooth, spongiform nodule.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Most nodules are benign colloid or hyperplastic nodules; stability, softness and a spongiform ultrasound are reassuring.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: benign or malignant?

clues: no weight loss or voice change
steps.x: Long-standing, stable, soft, no red flags, benign ultrasound features.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Benign colloid nodule**: most nodules are benign.

elim: Rapidly growing and hard, in the elderly.
Would not look spongiform; usually larger, solid.
Needs calcitonin or family history.
Hypoechoic with microcalcifications; she has none.

steps.x: **B. Benign colloid nodule.** No red flags + benign ultrasound = benign nodule.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman has a lump in the lower left side of her neck. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 116/74 mmHg. Ultrasound shows a solitary nodule in the left thyroid lobe.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
o: Lump lies in the posterior triangle
Lump rises on swallowing but not on tongue protrusion
practice.e: Thyroid nodules move with the larynx on swallowing but not on tongue protrusion, which distinguishes them from a thyroglossal cyst.

steps.x: An examination finding question.

clues: lower left side of her neck
solitary nodule in the left thyroid lobe
steps.x: A confirmed **thyroid** nodule.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The thyroid is attached to the larynx: it **moves on swallowing** but not with the tongue.

elim: Suggests a carotid aneurysm or body tumour.
Lateral to the thyroid: nodes or other lesions.
That is a thyroglossal cyst.
A cystic hygroma or other fluid-filled lesion.

steps.x: **C. Lump rises on swallowing but not on tongue protrusion.** Thyroid moves on swallowing; thyroglossal cyst also moves on tongue protrusion.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man has a hard nodule in his thyroid. His father had a thyroid operation and his brother had an adrenal tumour removed for episodes of palpitations and sweating. His BP is 168/102 mmHg and pulse rate 104 bpm.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Medullary carcinoma arises from calcitonin-secreting C cells and is linked to MEN 2 with phaeochromocytoma.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: the family history is the clue.

clues: adrenal tumour removed for episodes of palpitations and sweating
steps.x: Family history of thyroid cancer and **phaeochromocytoma**, hypertension, raised **calcitonin**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Medullary carcinoma** in **MEN 2**.

elim: Elderly, rapidly growing, compressive.
No calcitonin rise or family link.
Commonest, but calcitonin and MEN 2 family history point elsewhere.
TSH would be suppressed; calcitonin normal.

steps.x: **C. Medullary thyroid carcinoma.** Thyroid nodule + calcitonin + phaeo family history = medullary.

practice.stem: An 81 year old woman has a neck swelling that has grown rapidly over 4 weeks. She now has difficulty swallowing and noisy breathing. There is a hard, fixed mass in the thyroid with bilateral cervical lymphadenopathy. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Anaplastic carcinoma presents late in the elderly with a rapidly enlarging mass causing compressive symptoms.

steps.x: Diagnosis question: the speed and the age.
Elderly, rapid growth, local compression and lymphadenopathy.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Anaplastic carcinoma**: rarest, most aggressive.

elim: Slow growth over years, not weeks, and not fixed.
Slower; spreads by blood rather than local invasion.
No calcitonin or family history.
Younger patients, slow growth.

steps.x: **A. Anaplastic thyroid carcinoma.** Elderly + rapid hard compressive mass = anaplastic.

practice.stem: A 63 year old woman has a 4 cm thyroid nodule. She has had pain in her right hip for 2 months. X-ray shows a lytic lesion in the femur. Her pulse rate is 80 bpm and BP 132/84 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely type of thyroid cancer?
practice.e: Follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously to bone and lung; papillary spreads to lymph nodes.

steps.x: Which type: look at the pattern of spread.
Older woman, no nodes, a **bone metastasis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Follicular carcinoma**: haematogenous spread to bone and lung.

elim: Kills by local invasion; she has no compressive features.
Calcitonin is normal.
Spreads to nodes first; she has none.
Rapid diffuse enlargement, not a bone metastasis.

steps.x: **B. Follicular thyroid carcinoma.** Bone or lung metastases = follicular; nodes = papillary.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man has a hard, irregular thyroid mass. Over 6 weeks his voice has become hoarse and weak. He has lost 5 kg. His pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 130/82 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his hoarse voice?
o: Superior laryngeal nerve stretching by a goitre
practice.e: Hoarseness from recurrent laryngeal nerve infiltration is a malignancy red flag in a thyroid nodule.

steps.x: A cause question about a red flag.
Hard irregular mass, weight loss and new hoarseness: **malignant** nodule invading locally.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Recurrent laryngeal nerve** infiltration paralyses a vocal cord.

elim: Does not explain the hard mass or weight loss.
Causes voice fatigue, rarely persistent hoarseness, and no mass invasion.
Does not cause hoarseness.
From voice overuse, not malignancy.

steps.x: **B. Recurrent laryngeal nerve infiltration.** Thyroid mass + hoarseness = recurrent laryngeal nerve involvement: a red flag.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has a 2 cm thyroid nodule found on a carotid Doppler scan. She feels well. Her pulse rate is 70 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. Her TSH is 1.6 mU/L.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Ultrasound is first-line imaging and stratifies malignancy risk to decide on FNA.

steps.x: 'Next' investigation once TSH is known.
Normal TSH: not a hot nodule.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Dedicated thyroid ultrasound** to grade risk.

elim: Not first-line for nodule assessment.
Ultrasound decides whether FNA is needed and guides it.
Only if TSH is low.
Not a first-line test.

steps.x: **E. Ultrasound of the thyroid.** TSH normal → ultrasound; TSH low → scan.

practice.stem: A 55 year old woman has a 3 cm thyroid nodule, weight loss and palpitations. Her pulse rate is 108 bpm and BP 136/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: A low TSH suggests an autonomously functioning nodule; a radionuclide scan shows whether it is hot (benign) or cold.

steps.x: Next investigation with a thyrotoxic nodule.
Low TSH, high T4: the nodule may be **autonomous**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Radionuclide scan**: hot nodule = benign autonomous function.

elim: Does not show function.
Hot nodules are rarely malignant; scan first.
Not first-line.
Not indicated.

steps.x: **D. Radionuclide thyroid scan.** Low TSH + nodule → radionuclide scan.

practice.stem: A 50 year old woman has a 15 mm thyroid nodule. Her TSH is normal. Ultrasound features are benign and FNA cytology is benign. She has no compressive symptoms. Her BP is 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
practice.e: Benign, asymptomatic nodules with normal function are managed with reassurance and regular follow-up.

steps.x: Management of a benign result.
Normal function, benign ultrasound and benign cytology, no symptoms.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reassure and monitor**.

elim: Not needed for a benign, asymptomatic nodule.
Not recommended for benign nodules.
For hot toxic nodules or after cancer surgery.
For malignant nodules.

steps.x: **D. Reassurance and monitoring.** Benign nodule = reassurance and follow-up.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 25 mm thyroid nodule. FNA cytology is malignant, consistent with papillary carcinoma. Her pulse rate is 74 bpm and BP 116/70 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Malignant nodules need total or partial thyroidectomy, with radioactive iodine as secondary treatment.

steps.x: 'Definitive' management of a malignant nodule.
Cytology-proven papillary cancer.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Thyroidectomy**, then **radioactive iodine**.

elim: An antithyroid drug for hyperthyroidism.
Not primary treatment for papillary carcinoma.
Given after surgery, not instead of it.
Delays treatment of a confirmed cancer.

steps.x: **E. Thyroidectomy followed by radioactive iodine.** Malignant nodule → total or partial thyroidectomy, then RAI.

practice.stem: A 60 year old woman has palpitations and weight loss. She has a single thyroid nodule that is 'hot' on radionuclide scan, with suppression of the rest of the gland. Her pulse rate is 104 bpm and BP 138/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: A thyrotoxic hot nodule is treated by managing the hyperthyroidism, with radioiodine or surgery as options.

steps.x: Definitive management of a toxic nodule.
A **hot**, autonomously functioning nodule causing hyperthyroidism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Treat the hyperthyroidism: **radioiodine** (or surgery).

elim: Hot nodules are rarely malignant.
Treats symptoms, not the nodule.
She is thyrotoxic.
Cancer surgery; this is a benign toxic nodule.

steps.x: **C. Radioiodine.** Toxic nodule → radioiodine or surgery.

practice.stem: A 44 year old woman develops tingling around her mouth and in her fingertips 18 hours after a total thyroidectomy. Her voice is normal. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg. Tapping over her facial nerve causes twitching of her lip.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her symptoms?
o: Injury to the recurrent laryngeal nerve
practice.e: Injury to or devascularisation of the parathyroids during thyroidectomy causes hypocalcaemia with perioral paraesthesia.

steps.x: A mechanism question about a complication.
Perioral paraesthesia and **Chvostek's sign** after thyroidectomy: **hypocalcaemia**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: The **parathyroid glands** were injured or devascularised.

elim: Can cause tingling, but not after this operation with a positive Chvostek's sign.
Causes hoarseness; her voice is normal.
Causes swelling and stridor.
Fever, tachycardia, agitation; not perioral tingling.

steps.x: **A. Devascularisation of the parathyroid glands.** Perioral tingling after thyroidectomy = parathyroid injury → low calcium.
